lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: So you've finally come to join us too, Polystratus? I suppose you lived not much less than a hundred years?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Ninety-eight, Simylus.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: How did you manage those thirty years after me? I died when you were around seventy.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Most delightfully, even if that seems odd to you.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Odd, if as an old, weak, childless man you could still enjoy life.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: At first, I could do everything. There were still plenty of handsome boys, the most delicate women, perfumes, the finest wines, and a table that put Sicilian ones to shame.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: That's new. I knew you as very frugal.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: But the good things flowed in from others, my good man. From dawn, crowds would flock to my door, and from all over the world the finest gifts were brought to me.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Did you become a tyrant after I left, Polystratus?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: No, but I had thousands of lovers.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: [laughs] You had lovers at your age, with only four teeth?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: By Zeus, the best men in the city. Old and bald as you see me, toothless and runny-nosed besides, they delighted in serving me, and whichever one I glanced at even once considered himself blessed.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Did you perhaps ferry someone like Phaon did Aphrodite from Chios, and then she granted your wish to be young and beautiful again and worth loving?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: No, but even as I was, I was passionately desired.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: You're talking in riddles.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: But it's perfectly clear: this kind of love is common for childless and wealthy old men.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Now I understand your beauty, my dear fellow — it was from golden Aphrodite.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: And yet, Simylus, I enjoyed no small number of my lovers, who almost worshipped me. I often played coy and sometimes shut my door on some of them, but they competed and outdid each other in their eagerness to please me.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: In the end, how did you decide about your property?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: In public, I said I would leave each of them as my heir, and each one believed it and made himself even more flattering. But I had other, true wills, and left them all to their own devices, telling them to go hang.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Who did the final ones make heir? Some relative, I suppose?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: No, by Zeus, but a young Phrygian slave, one of the handsome boys.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: About how old, Polystratus?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Around twenty.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Now I see what he was doing for you.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Still, he was far more deserving to inherit than they were, even if he was a barbarian and a scoundrel — the very best men are serving him now. So he inherited from me, and now he's counted among the nobility, with his beard shaved, still speaking broken Greek, but said to be nobler than Codrus, more beautiful than Nireus, and wiser than Odysseus.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: I don't care. Let him even command the Greeks if he likes — as long as those others don't inherit.
